changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
changes.change: For engineering-led buyers: "Payments shouldn't be a team. Have one of your engineers build your own payment flow in our sandbox this week, and see it working before you decide." Put the sandbox build in the first meeting as the call to action, not behind the slides. For two-sided apps, name the flow with their word for their supply side (e.g. 'sitter pay').
changes.why: The deal turned when an engineer built a working sitter payment flow in the sandbox on her own (E17), after which the decider stopped saying 'if' (E23). The docs and sandbox were what got a reaction (E16), and 'Payments shouldn't be a team' (E35) is the customer's sharper version of our developer pitch.

changes.current_line: Onboard, verify and pay out to sellers worldwide, in their local currency.
changes.change: For two-sided apps such as pet care and services: "Onboard and verify your sitters, and pay them locally in every country you launch, without babysitting the code." Swap 'sitters' for the customer's own name for their supply side. Avoid 'marketplace', 'sellers' and 'payouts'. Do not promise a payout timing like 'paid by Friday' until we have confirmed it.
changes.why: The marketplace onboarding, identity checks and local-currency payouts landed (E19) because expansion meant sitters had to be paid locally (E1). The customer never says 'payouts', they say 'sitter pay' (E40), and they describe the burden as 'babysitting' (E36). Whether sitter pay timing changes is still unconfirmed, so no timing claim is included.

changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For low-ticket, two-sided apps, stop leading with the authorization-rate slide. Use it only if the buyer raises acceptance, and then with their own numbers rather than our average.
changes.why: The acceptance-rate slide drew silence (E20), and the decider dismissed it outright: 'our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates' (E21).

changes.change: For switch deals against an incumbent, add a 'What you keep' proof point to use before talking about speed. It should give a confirmed statement on PayPal and Venmo button continuity, plus a saved-card migration reference from a customer of comparable size. Do not publish this until product confirms the Venmo answer and a reference is sourced. The working line, once confirmed: "Switch without losing what your customers use: keep PayPal and Venmo, and bring your saved cards with you."
changes.why: The evaluation shifted from 'how fast can we build this' to 'what do we lose' (E13) over wallets and saved cards (E11). The rep had no Venmo answer (E27) and no peer proof for 'who's done this at our size without losing cards?' (E31), and both questions are still open after signature.
